description: We’re Team DeltaX: curious minds, questionable sleep schedules and a dangerous amount of caffeine, turning big space problems into bold ideas. We build, debate, test, break, fix and repeat because apparently “good enough” was never our thing.
summary:
Across Bangladesh, a farmer's most consequential decisions often begin with a deceptively simple question: what can this land grow, and when? TurningTides (জমির ডাক্তার) is a nationwide, satellite-powered agricultural intelligence platform developed to answer that question with scientific evidence.

Covering 5,160 union-level administrative units, it integrates Earth-observation imagery with soil, terrain, rainfall and climate data to transform the environmental characteristics of a particular location into actionable agricultural guidance. Farmers can identify or delineate their land, assess the suitability of different crops, discover optimal planting windows and varieties, evaluate seasonal hazards, compare crop rotations and receive practical, seven-day cultivation plans.

Its specialised systems address region-specific threats, from flash floods in the haor basin to salinity across the coastal belt. Designed for accessibility beyond smartphones, the platform also incorporates a low-bandwidth interface, an SMS-based prototype and printable Land Cards.

By translating complex satellite observations into intelligible, location-specific decisions, TurningTides seeks to make agricultural intelligence accessible to every farmer, irrespective of location or technological means.
details:
Bangladesh is one delta, yet its agricultural realities are remarkably different. In the north-eastern haors, flash floods can destroy months of cultivation days before Boro rice reaches harvest. Along the south-western coast, residual soil salinity can jeopardise entire planting seasons. Across the north, cold spells threaten seedbeds, while other regions face water scarcity, flooding and increasingly unpredictable weather. The problem is not simply a lack of agricultural information; it is the absence of sufficiently precise, timely and accessible intelligence for the individual farmer. TurningTides (জমির ডাক্তার), developed by Team Delta X, addresses this challenge by transforming decades of satellite observations and environmental data into actionable agricultural decisions.

How it works

TurningTides constructs a month-by-month environmental profile across all 64 districts and 5,160 union-level administrative units in Bangladesh. These profiles encompass temperature extremes, precipitation, soil texture and acidity, standing water, flood exposure and coastal salinity. Its geographical framework provides spatial resolution as fine as 250 metres across eight flagship districts and 1 kilometre elsewhere, with explicit confidence indicators.

The platform incorporates 44 crops, drawing their environmental requirements from FAO ECOCROP and FAO agricultural references, while planting calendars and recommended varieties are informed by BRRI, BARI and other Bangladesh-specific agricultural sources.

A farmer can locate their land through geographical search or GPS, or delineate an individual plot on an interactive satellite and terrain map. The Crop Check engine then evaluates up to six environmental dimensions: temperature, rainfall and water availability, soil characteristics, soil acidity, salinity and flooding. Its distinctive weakest-factor decision logic ensures that a severely limiting condition cannot be concealed by favourable scores elsewhere. The outcome is an intelligible green, amber or red verdict: Yes, grow it; Possible with care; or Not here, not now. Each verdict is accompanied by its underlying reasoning, Bangla planting windows, suitable varieties, seasonal hazards and alternative crops.

Beyond crop selection, Season Plan compares cultivation rotations and evaluates their historical performance through a Time Machine. Weather Guard translates weather information and historical risk patterns into practical cultivation guidance, while Region Guardians identify threats particular to different geographical regions.

NASA-powered scientific innovation

NASA Earth-observation resources underpin several of the platform's most important analytical capabilities. GPM IMERG precipitation records (2001–2025) inform rainfall climatology, hazardous-weather analysis and the Flush Clock. NASA POWER climate records (1991–2025) support historical temperature assessments and rainfall analysis over the upstream Meghalaya slopes that feed the haor river systems. NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble, accessed through GIBS, provide geographical visualisation backdrops.

These datasets are complemented by Landsat-derived JRC Global Surface Water records (1984–2021), Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar observations (2015–2025), Sentinel-2 imagery, SoilGrids 2.0, laboratory soil-salinity samples, Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics records and agricultural research from FAO, BRRI and BARI.

Two specialised systems demonstrate the project's scientific depth.

Harvest Race, developed for the Sunamganj haor region, monitors three-day accumulated rainfall over upstream hills. When rainfall exceeds its 165 mm threshold, the system generates an early-harvest warning. Its historical hindcast identified three of five early-flood events in time, providing 8, 7 and 11 days of advance warning respectively. It missed the 2015 and 2022 events and generated no false alarms across the 11 assessed seasons. These limitations remain visible in the platform.

Flush Clock addresses coastal salinity across 267 south-western unions. It estimates how accumulated monsoon rainfall can leach residual soil salts beneath the root zone and identifies a potentially safe period for transplanting Aman rice. In a held-out assessment covering 452 saline union-years from 2021–2025, planting occurred on or after the estimated safe date in 85% of cases, compared with 54% using the published planting rule alone. Each estimate carries an individual confidence assessment.

The broader crop-suitability engine has also been evaluated against agricultural statistics: 247 of 252 major-district crop assessments agreed with the corresponding crop-area patterns in BBS 2021–22 records.

Accessibility and intended impact

TurningTides was designed around a fundamental principle: scientific intelligence should not be restricted by a farmer's device or internet connection. Its three experience tiers provide a comprehensive standard interface, a Lite experience with a measured first-load size of 215.8 KB under emulated 2G conditions, and simplified access through an SMS command-and-response system. Printable Land Cards provide another route through which agricultural officers and Union Digital Centres can assist farmers with location-specific information. The application also supports offline access after the initial visit.

The project's field deployment has now been completed, bringing the developed system beyond the conceptual stage and into its intended real-world setting. Its intended long-term impact is to improve agricultural decision-making, reduce preventable cultivation losses, encourage more appropriate use of land and water resources, and strengthen resilience against increasingly variable environmental conditions.

Technology, creativity and development considerations

The project combines Python-based geospatial processing, scientific computation and data engineering with a TypeScript and Preact web application. Its interface and geographical infrastructure employ HTML, CSS, MapLibre GL, Three.js and D3. Scientific processing uses libraries including NumPy, Pandas, Xarray, Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, SciPy and Scikit-learn. STAC-based satellite-data discovery, Cloud Optimised GeoTIFFs, static JSON bundles and PMTiles support efficient geographical data delivery. No specialised agricultural hardware is required.

What makes TurningTides distinctive is not simply its incorporation of satellite data, but the way it connects national-scale environmental intelligence, individual land assessment, explainable crop recommendations, historical scenario testing and multiple accessibility channels through a unified decision-making framework. The team considered geographical diversity, scientific uncertainty, data provenance, spatial resolution, affordability, unreliable connectivity, language accessibility and the practical circumstances of agricultural communities throughout its development.

The underlying ambition is to make the distance between observing the Earth and helping someone cultivate it considerably smaller: transforming what satellites can see into what farmers can understand, decide and act upon.
